concepts.title: Finding your way around
concepts.lede: The shell is a text conversation with your computer. You always stand in one directory, and a few commands let you look around and move.

blocks.x:
$ pwd                  # print working directory: where am I?
/home/ana/projects
$ ls                   # list files here
reviewradar  notes.txt
$ ls -la               # long format, including hidden files (names starting with .)
$ cd reviewradar       # move into a folder
$ cd ..                # up one level
$ cd ~                 # your home folder (also just: cd)
$ cd /                 # the very top
A path that starts with `/` is **absolute**: it works from anywhere. Anything else is **relative** to where you are standing.
Press **Tab** to auto-complete names and the up arrow to bring back earlier commands. `command --help` and `man command` explain flags.

blocks.q: You are in `/home/ana/projects`. Where does `cd ../..` take you?
blocks.why: Each `..` goes up one level: projects, then ana, landing in /home.

exercises.prompt: What does this print? (`basename` shows only the last part of the path.)
hints: Track which folder you are in after each `cd`.
`..` goes to the parent folder.
First `proj/data`, then up and into `src`, then up to `proj`.
exercises.code:
mkdir -p proj/data proj/src
cd proj/data
cd ../src
basename "$PWD"
cd ..
basename "$PWD"

exercises.prompt: You are in `/home/ana/projects/reviewradar/src`. Which command returns you to `/home/ana`?
hints: `~` is a shortcut.
Count the folders if you use `..`: src, reviewradar, projects.
`cd ~` goes to your home, and `cd ../../..` also works here.
whys: That reaches /home/ana only because the path is exactly three levels deep.
`.` is the folder you are already in.

hints: `-l` means long format.

concepts.title: Working with files and globs
concepts.lede: Create, copy, move and delete from the command line, and use wildcards (globs) to act on many files at once.

blocks.x:
$ mkdir logs                 # new folder
$ touch notes.txt            # new empty file
$ cp notes.txt backup.txt    # copy
$ mv backup.txt logs/        # move (also renames: mv old new)
$ rm notes.txt               # delete a file (no recycle bin!)
$ rm -r old_folder           # delete a folder and everything in it
$ ls *.csv                   # * matches any text
$ ls report?.csv             # ? matches exactly one character
$ cat notes.txt              # print a file; less notes.txt to page through it
`rm` has no undo. Be careful with `rm -r`, and never run `rm -rf` with a path you have not double-checked. A stray space in `rm * .log` deletes **everything** and then looks for a file called `.log`.

x: The **shell** expands `*.csv` into a list of file names before the command runs.
Quote names with spaces: `cp "my file.txt" backup/`.
`mv` renames when the target is a new name in the same folder.

blocks.q: Which pattern matches `report1.csv` and `report2.csv` but not `report10.csv`?

hints: `ls` lists names in alphabetical order.

concepts.title: Pipes and redirection
concepts.lede: Small tools that each do one thing become powerful when you connect them. A pipe `|` feeds one command's output into the next.

blocks.x:
cat access.log | grep 404 | wc -l       # how many 404s?
echo "first" > out.txt                  # > overwrite a file
echo "second" >> out.txt                # >> append to a file
wc -l < out.txt                         # < read a file as input
command 2> errors.txt                   # 2> sends error messages to a file
command > all.txt 2>&1                  # stdout and stderr to the same place

x: `sort`, `uniq -c` (count adjacent duplicates), `head`, `tail`, `wc -l`, `cut -d, -f2` are the everyday toolbox.
`uniq` only collapses **adjacent** duplicates, so sort first.
`>` truncates the file first. Use `>>` to add to the end.

choices: Sends error output to the same place as normal output
blocks.why: File descriptor 2 is stderr and 1 is stdout.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
hints: `sort` puts equal lines next to each other.

`sort -rn` puts the largest count first and `head -1` keeps one line.

printf 'bug
billing
bug
feature

' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -1

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
hints: `>` replaces the file's contents.
Only the last write survives.
So the file has one line.

explain.ask: In your own words: why is `first` gone from the file?
explain.model: A single `>` opens the file for writing from scratch, wiping what was there. Only `>>` adds to the end. The final `echo "third" > out.txt` therefore left a one-line file.

exercises.code:

echo "second" >> out.txt
echo "third" > out.txt
cat out.txt

hints: One redirection overwrites, another adds.

concepts.title: Searching with grep and find
concepts.lede: `grep` finds lines that match a pattern. `find` finds files by name, type or age. Together they answer most "where is it?" questions.

blocks.x:
grep ERROR app.log                  # lines containing ERROR
grep -c ERROR app.log               # just the count
grep -n timeout app.log             # show line numbers
grep -v INFO app.log                # lines that do NOT match
grep -i "error" app.log             # ignore case
grep -r "TODO" src/                 # search every file under src/
grep -E 'ERROR|WARN' app.log        # extended regex: either word

find . -name "*.py"                 # files by name
find . -type f -mtime -1            # files changed in the last day

x: `-i` ignore case, `-v` invert, `-n` line numbers, `-c` count, `-r` recursive, `-l` just file names.
Quote patterns so the shell does not expand them first.
Pipe into `grep` to filter any command's output: `ps aux | grep python`.

blocks.q: Which command counts the lines that contain `ERROR`?
blocks.why: `-c` prints the number of matching lines.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
hints: The log has 5 lines; two contain ERROR.
`-v` keeps lines without INFO.
`-n` prefixes the line number and a colon.
exercises.code:

grep -v INFO app.log | head -2
grep -n timeout app.log
exercises.answer:
2
ERROR disk full
WARN slow
4:ERROR timeout

hints: You need two flags: recursive and case-insensitive.
`-r` recurses, `-i` ignores case.
`-ri`

concepts.title: sed: edit streams of text
concepts.lede: `sed` rewrites text as it flows past. Its most useful trick is substitution: `s/old/new/`.

x: The form is `s/pattern/replacement/flags`. Use another separator when the text has slashes: `s#/old/path#/new/path#`.
`-n` plus `p` prints only the lines you select.
`-i` edits the file **in place**. Adding `.bak` keeps the original.

blocks.x: `sed -i` changes the file directly. Try the command without `-i` first, or keep a `.bak` copy.

choices: Replaces every match on a line, not just the first
blocks.why: Without `g`, only the first match in each line is replaced.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
hints: Without `g` only the first match per line changes.
With `g` every match changes.
The input is the same for both.
exercises.code:
echo "bug in bug fix" | sed 's/bug/issue/'
echo "bug in bug fix" | sed 's/bug/issue/g'
exercises.answer:
issue in bug fix
issue in issue fix

hints: The pattern goes first, the replacement second.

hints: `-n` suppresses normal output.

concepts.title: awk: work with columns
concepts.lede: `awk` splits each line into fields (`$1`, `$2`, ...) and runs a small program on each. It is perfect for logs and tables.

blocks.x:
awk '{print $1}' sales.txt                      # first column
awk '$2 > 6 {print $1}' sales.txt               # only rows where column 2 is above 6
awk -F, '{print $2}' data.csv                   # -F sets the field separator
awk 'NR == 2 {print $1}' sales.txt              # NR = current line number
awk '{sum[$1] += $2} END {for (k in sum) print k, sum[k]}' sales.txt   # total per name

x: `$0` is the whole line, `$NF` the last field, `NR` the line number, `NF` the number of fields.
`BEGIN { }` runs before the first line, `END { }` after the last.
Associative arrays (`sum[$1]`) are awk's dictionaries.

choices: Makes the comma the field separator
blocks.why: `-F` chooses the separator, so lines split at commas.

exercises.prompt: What does this print? (the output is sorted)
hints: `s[$1] += $2` adds column 2 into a bucket named by column 1.
The `END` block prints each total.
exercises.code: awk '{s[$1] += $2} END {for (k in s) print k, s[k]}' sales.txt | sort

exercises.prompt: Print the first column of rows whose second column is greater than 6.
hints: Fields are numbered from 1.
The name is in the first column.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
hints: `NR == 2` selects the second line.
The second line is `ben 5`.
The total of column 2 is 10 + 5 + 7 + 8.
exercises.code:

awk '{n += $2} END {print n}' sales.txt

concepts.title: Environment variables and quoting
concepts.lede: Variables carry configuration into programs. Quotes decide whether the shell expands them. Both matter for secrets and for ReviewRadar's config.

blocks.x:
NAME=ana                          # no spaces around =
echo "hi $NAME"                   # hi ana        (double quotes expand variables)
echo 'hi $NAME'                   # hi $NAME      (single quotes do not)
export STAGE=prod                 # make it visible to programs you start
bash -c 'echo $STAGE'             # prod
DB_HOST=localhost python app.py   # set a variable for one command only
echo $PATH                        # folders searched for commands

x: A plain variable lives only in the current shell. `export` passes it on to child processes.
`$PATH` lists where the shell looks for commands. `which python` shows which one it found.
Secrets such as API keys belong in environment variables or a secret store, **never** in code or git.

blocks.x: Always quote variables that may contain spaces: `"$file"`, not `$file`. Unquoted values get split into several words.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
hints: Double quotes expand, single quotes do not.
A child `bash` only sees exported variables.
`OTHER` was never exported.

explain.ask: In your own words: why is `OTHER` empty in the child shell?
points: Only exported variables are passed to child processes
OTHER was set without export so it stays in the parent shell
explain.model: A plain assignment creates a shell variable that only the current shell can see. `export` marks it for inheritance, so child processes receive a copy.

exercises.code:
NAME=ana
echo "hi $NAME" 'hi $NAME'
export STAGE=prod
bash -c 'echo $STAGE'
OTHER=x
bash -c 'echo "[$OTHER]"'

exercises.prompt: This should print `Price is 5`, but it prints the text `Price is $price`. Which line is the problem?
hints: Look at the type of quotes.
Single quotes stop the shell from expanding variables.
Switch to double quotes.

choices: Remove the quotes: `echo Price is $price` is the only option

concepts.title: Writing shell scripts
concepts.lede: A script is a text file of commands. Add a shebang, a few variables and a loop, and repetitive work becomes one command.

blocks.x:
#!/bin/bash                       # which program runs this file
name=${1:-world}                  # first argument, default "world"
for f in *.csv; do                # loop over files
    echo "processing $f"
done
if [ -f "$name" ]; then           # test: is it a regular file?
    echo "exists"
fi
count=$(wc -l < data.txt)         # capture a command's output
echo "$count lines"

x: Make it runnable once with `chmod +x script.sh`, then start it with `./script.sh arg1 arg2`.
`$1`, `$2` are arguments, `$@` is all of them, `$#` is how many. `$(cmd)` captures output.
Tests live in `[ ... ]`: `-f` file, `-d` folder, `-z` empty string, `-eq` numbers equal, `==` strings equal. **Spaces inside the brackets are required.**

blocks.x: Unquoted variables break on spaces. If `file="my report.txt"`, then `rm $file` runs `rm my report.txt` and tries to delete two files. Write `rm "$file"`.

blocks.why: `$0` is the name, `$1` the first argument, `$#` the count.

exercises.prompt: The file `greet.sh` below is run as `bash greet.sh ana` and then as `bash greet.sh`. What is printed in total?
hints: `${1:-world}` means: the first argument, or `world` if there is none.
The loop runs twice for each run.
First run uses `ana`, the second uses `world`.
exercises.answer:
hello ana 1
hello ana 2
hello world 1
hello world 2

exercises.prompt: Put the lines in order to back up every CSV into a `backup` folder and then print `done`.
hints: The shebang is always the first line.
Create the folder before copying into it.
The loop body sits between `do` and `done`.

exercises.prompt: This script should delete `my report.txt`, but it fails with two errors. Which line is the problem?
hints: Compare how line 2 and line 3 use the variable.
Unquoted variables are split at spaces.
Line 3 runs `rm my report.txt`.

why: `-f` hides the error but still tries to delete two wrong files.
Single quotes pass the literal text `$file`.
That deletes a file literally called `file`.

exercises.prompt: Complete the test.
hints: An `if` in bash is closed by `fi`. What keyword opens its body?
It comes after the semicolon.
`then`

concepts.title: Exit codes and safe scripts
concepts.lede: Every command ends with a number: 0 means success, anything else means failure. Safe scripts check it, and stop when something goes wrong.

blocks.x:
true;  echo $?          # 0   ($? is the last exit code)
false; echo $?          # 1

mkdir build && cd build        # && : run the next only if the first succeeded
cmd1 || echo "cmd1 failed"     # || : run the next only if the first failed

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail              # e: stop on error, u: error on unset variables, pipefail: a failing pipe step fails the whole pipe
trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT       # always clean up, even on error
cd "$BUILD_DIR" || exit 1      # never carry on in the wrong folder

x: CI systems judge a job by its exit code. Exit 0 means pass, so a script that swallows errors makes CI lie.
`set -e` stops at the first failing command. `set -u` catches typos in variable names.
`exit 3` ends the script with your own code.

blocks.x: `cd "$DIR"` followed by `rm -rf ./*` is a famous disaster: if `cd` fails, the `rm` runs in the wrong folder. Guard with `cd "$DIR" || exit 1`.

choices: Stops the script when a command fails
blocks.why: The script exits as soon as a command returns non-zero.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
hints: `&&` runs the right side only after success.
`||` runs the right side only after failure.
`test -f nofile` fails, so `$?` is 1.
exercises.code:
true && echo A
false && echo B
false || echo C
test -f nofile; echo $?

exercises.prompt: A CI step runs `./deploy.sh`. The script's last command fails but the script ends with `echo finished`. What exit code does the script return, and what does CI show?
hints: A script's exit code is the exit code of its last command.
`echo` succeeds.
Use `set -e` so the failure stops the script.
choices: 0, CI passes even though something failed

exercises.prompt: This cleanup script deletes the wrong files when `$BUILD_DIR` does not exist. Which line is the problem?
hints: What happens to line 3 if line 2 fails?
Without protection the script keeps going.
It would delete everything in the current folder.

choices: Wrap the path in single quotes

exercises.prompt: Make the script always remove the temp file when it ends, even after an error.
hints: `trap` runs a command when a signal or event happens.
There is a pseudo-signal for "the script is ending".
`EXIT`

concepts.title: Log forensics with one-liners
concepts.lede: When a service misbehaves at 3 a.m., the answer is in the logs. A few pipelines answer almost every question: how many, which, how slow, from whom.

blocks.x: A web log with the fields `ip method path status milliseconds`. Tap through a typical investigation: how often does each status code appear?

data.title: Count requests by status
data.input:
10.0.0.1 GET /predict 200 120
10.0.0.2 POST /predict 500 340
10.0.0.1 GET /health 200 3
10.0.0.3 POST /predict 200 150
10.0.0.2 POST /predict 500 360
10.0.0.1 GET /predict 404 8

stages.out:
10.0.0.1 GET /predict 200 120
10.0.0.2 POST /predict 500 340
10.0.0.1 GET /health 200 3
10.0.0.3 POST /predict 200 150
10.0.0.2 POST /predict 500 360
10.0.0.1 GET /predict 404 8

blocks.x:
awk '$4 == 500 {s += $5; n++} END {print s / n}' access.log     # average ms of the 500s
awk '$3 == "/predict" && $4 >= 500 {print $1}' access.log | sort -u   # who hit errors
sort -k5 -nr access.log | head -3                                # 3 slowest requests
grep -c " 500 " access.log                                       # how many errors
tail -f app.log | grep --line-buffered ERROR                     # watch live

x: Think in three steps: **select** the lines (`grep`, `awk` condition), **extract** the field (`awk '{print $n}'`, `cut`), **summarise** (`sort | uniq -c`, `awk` sums, `wc -l`).
`sort -k5 -n` sorts by the 5th field numerically. `-r` reverses.
`sort -u` is `sort | uniq`.

blocks.q: Which pipeline lists each distinct IP once?
blocks.why: `uniq` only removes adjacent duplicates, so sort first. `sort -u` does both.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
hints: Column 4 is the status code.
`uniq -c` counts each distinct code after sorting.
`sort -rn` puts the most common first.
exercises.code: awk '{print $4}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

hints: Only lines whose status is 500 are summed.
Their times are 340 and 360.
Divide the total by the count.

concepts.title: Makefile basics
concepts.lede: A Makefile names the commands you run all the time (`make test`, `make lint`, `make docker`) so everyone, and CI, runs them the same way.

blocks.x:
GREETING = hello                     # a variable

.PHONY: test lint all                # these names are tasks, not files

all: lint test                       # default target: runs these first

test:                                # target:
	pytest -q                          #   recipe (must start with a TAB)

lint:
	ruff check .

docker:
	docker build -t reviewradar:$(TAG) .

x: `target: prerequisites` followed by recipe lines indented with a **TAB**, not spaces.
`make` with no argument runs the first target. `make test` runs `test`.
`.PHONY` says the target is a task. Without it, a file called `test` would make `make test` think the work is already done.
Inside recipes `$@` is the target name and `$<` the first prerequisite. Variables are read with `$(NAME)`.

blocks.x: Recipes indented with spaces fail with `missing separator`. Configure your editor to insert a real tab in Makefiles.

blocks.q: What does `.PHONY: test` protect you from?
choices: A file named `test` making `make test` do nothing
blocks.why: Make skips a target whose file already exists and is up to date; `.PHONY` forces the recipe to run.

exercises.prompt: Given this Makefile, what does `make` (no arguments) print? (Recipe lines start with a tab.)
hints: `make` runs the first target, `all`.
`all` depends on `build`, so `build` runs first.
`$(GREETING)` expands to `hello`. `@` hides the command itself.

exercises.prompt: Declare the targets that are tasks rather than files.
hints: The name is spelled in capitals, after a dot.
It means "these targets are not files".
`.PHONY`
exercises.template:
.____: test lint
test:
	pytest -q
lint:
	ruff check .

exercises.prompt: In a recipe, what does `$@` stand for?
hints: It is an automatic variable.
Think of it as "at the target".
`$<` is the first prerequisite.
choices: The name of the target being built

concepts.title: Shell in CI and automation
concepts.lede: CI pipelines are mostly shell. A few patterns (`xargs`, loops, strict flags, `curl --fail`) cover most automation you will write.

blocks.x:
printf 'a.txt\nb.txt\n' | xargs -I{} echo "file: {}"     # run a command once per input line
find . -name "*.pyc" -delete                             # find and delete
for f in a b; do echo "run $f"; done | wc -l             # 2

curl -sf https://api.example.com/health || exit 1        # -s quiet, -f fail on HTTP errors
docker build -t app . && docker push app                 # push only if build succeeded
set -x                                                   # echo every command (do NOT use with secrets)

x: `&&` chains steps that depend on each other. `;` runs the next step regardless, which is rarely what CI wants.
Never print secrets. CI masks known secrets, but `set -x` or `echo "$TOKEN"` can still leak derived values.
Use `jq` to read JSON from APIs: `curl -s url | jq -r .status`.

blocks.q: You want to push a Docker image only if the build worked. Which is right?
blocks.why: `&&` stops the chain when the build fails.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
hints: `xargs -I{}` runs the command once per input line.
The loop prints three lines.
`wc -l` counts them.
exercises.code:
printf 'a.txt\nb.txt\n' | xargs -I{} echo "file: {}"
for f in a b c; do echo "run $f"; done | wc -l

exercises.prompt: This CI script pushes an image even when the build fails. Which line is the problem?
hints: Look at how the two commands are joined.
A semicolon ignores the result of the first command.
Use `&&`, or add `set -e` at the top.
lines: docker build -t app . ; docker push app

choices: Swap the order of the commands

exercises.prompt: Make `curl` quiet and make it fail on HTTP errors, so a failed health check fails the job.
hints: `-s` silences the progress meter.
`-f` makes HTTP errors (like 500) return a non-zero exit code.
`-sf`

concepts.title: Scheduling and background jobs
concepts.lede: Batch scoring, backups and drift reports run on a schedule. Cron is simple and unforgiving: know its syntax and its quirks.

blocks.x:
# minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week   command
*/15 * * * *   /srv/reviewradar/score.sh        # every 15 minutes
30 2 * * *     /srv/reviewradar/backup.sh       # every day at 02:30
0 3 * * 1      /srv/reviewradar/drift.sh        # Mondays at 03:00 (0 or 7 = Sunday)
0 */6 * * *    /srv/reviewradar/report.sh       # every 6 hours, on the hour

crontab -e          # edit your schedule
crontab -l          # list it

x: Cron runs jobs with a **minimal environment**: a short `PATH`, no virtualenv, and your home as the working directory. Use absolute paths and `cd` in the command.
Capture output, or it vanishes: `>> /var/log/job.log 2>&1`.
A long job can overlap with its next run. Guard with `flock -n /tmp/job.lock command`.
In the shell: `cmd &` runs in the background, `jobs` lists, `wait` pauses until they finish, `nohup cmd &` survives closing the terminal, `kill PID` stops one.

blocks.x: "It works in my terminal but not in cron" is almost always the environment: the PATH, the working directory or a missing activated virtualenv.

blocks.q: Which schedule runs a job every day at 02:30?

exercises.prompt: Complete the cron expression for "every day at 02:30".
hints: The first field is the minute, the second is the hour.
02:30 means minute 30, hour 2.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
hints: `&` starts `sleep` in the background and the script moves on.
`wait` blocks until background jobs end.
So the order of the two echo lines is fixed.
exercises.code:
sleep 0.1 &
echo "started"
wait
echo "finished"

exercises.prompt: This cron job works when typed in a terminal but never produces output when scheduled. Which line is the problem?
hints: What is the working directory and `PATH` under cron?
The script path and interpreter are relative.
Cron also throws away output unless you redirect it.

why: `sudo` does not fix paths and adds risk.
That changes the schedule, not the problem.

exercises.prompt: Your hourly cron job sometimes takes 70 minutes, so two copies overlap and corrupt a file. What is the standard fix?
hints: The second copy should not start while the first still runs.
A file lock enforces that.
`flock -n` exits immediately when the lock is taken.
choices: Wrap it in a lock, for example `flock -n /tmp/job.lock ./job.sh`
